title: An Inspector Calls: the Inspector and Eva Smith
specPoints: Paper 2 Section A: modern drama, An Inspector Calls
AO2: a character as a dramatic device

tips.title: The one body line, exactly
tips.body: We don't live alone. We are members of one body. We are responsible for each other. Three short sentences; learn them as one unit, with the Act. It is the thesis of the play and it fits almost every question set on it.

tips.title: The four methods the scheme names
tips.body: Forensic questioning; directness against the family's evasiveness; the structural contrast before and after his arrival; the stage directions about him. Any essay on the Inspector can take two of these and name them as methods.

tips.title: Effect, not identity
tips.body: Ghost, conscience, Priestley's voice, device: the play supports all four. The mark is for what the uncertainty does, so write *whether he is read as a ghost or as Priestley's voice, he is built to be believed and then doubted*, and move on.

tips.title: The speech in four pieces
tips.body: Verdict, scale, principle, warning: helped to kill her; millions of Eva Smiths; members of one body; fire and blood and anguish. Four pieces are easier to carry than one long speech, and each answers a different kind of question.

tips.title: She is a device, not a victim to pity
tips.body: A paragraph that pities Eva Smith earns little. A paragraph that says why Priestley keeps her off stage, what the photograph does, and why her name is Smith, earns a great deal. Write what the writer does with her.

tips.title: Her two clean acts
tips.body: The strike for higher wages, and the refusal of money once she knew it was stolen. The girl the family dismissed is the most principled person in the play, and Priestley arranged that.

why.matters: The Inspector and the girl are the two characters Priestley invented most freely, and they are where his argument is made. One is on stage almost throughout, asking questions in an order that is itself a proof; the other never appears, and is known only through the people who failed her. Between them they carry the idea the play exists to put to its audience, that responsibility is shared and a society can be organised as one body. The June 2024 paper asked how Priestley uses the Inspector to suggest the need for social change, and a question on either of them is likely in any series. Reading them as devices, not people, is what the mark scheme rewards.

examples.title: The interrogation scene
examples.body: Every detective drama has a version of the Inspector: the questioner who already knows, who takes the suspects one at a time, and whose calm is more frightening than a raised voice. Watching one, the audience is doing what Priestley's audience does, judging the people questioned by how they answer. The difference in the play is that the questioner may not exist, so the last judgement is left to the family and to us.

examples.title: The person who is talked about but never seen
examples.body: Films and novels often build a character entirely out of what others say: the missing sister, the dead friend, the founder whose portrait hangs in the hall. What each speaker says about the absent person is evidence about the speaker. Priestley's girl is the cleanest example there is, and once the trick is seen it is visible in a great deal of other writing.

steps.title: Inspector Goole: how he works
steps.body:
The Inspector arrives in the middle of Birling's confidence, and from then on the evening is his. Priestley gives him a method and lets the audience watch it.

**One at a time.** He takes the five in the order they met the girl, and he does not move on until the link is admitted. He shows the photograph to one person at a time, so nobody can compare notes. The June 2024 mark scheme calls this his forensic questioning, and it names the contrast between his directness and the family's evasiveness as one of Priestley's methods.

**He does not argue; he states.** When Birling reminds him that he is a public man, the answer is a sentence, not a debate: “Public men, Mr Birling, have responsibilities as well as privileges” (the Inspector, Act 2). When the family try to keep the girl at a distance, Sheila sees that it is useless: “he knows” (Sheila, Act 2).

**Before and after.** The scheme also lists the structural contrast before and after his arrival. The room is the same; the lighting, the talk and the confidence are not. Everything he does is a method Priestley chose, and the essay question about him will ask what those methods are for.

steps.title: What the Inspector says: the speech
steps.body:
The Inspector's last speech is the play's argument, and Priestley gives it to him whole. Its parts are worth knowing separately, because each does a different job.

**The verdict:** “each of you helped to kill her” (the Inspector, Act 3). Not one of them killed her; each of them helped. That is the idea of shared responsibility in one sentence.

**The scale:** there are “millions and millions and millions of Eva Smiths”. The girl was one case; the point is every case. Eva and John Smith are the commonest names the play could choose.

**The principle:** “We don't live alone. We are members of one body. We are responsible for each other” (the Inspector, Act 3). This is the line to learn exactly. It is the opposite of Birling's speech in Act 1, and Priestley means the audience to hear the two against each other.

**The warning:** if the lesson is not learned, they will be taught it “in fire and blood and anguish”. To a family in 1912 it sounds like a preacher. To an audience in 1945 it is the history they have just lived through, twice.

Earlier lines prepare it: “have to share our guilt” (the Inspector, Act 2), and, to the family arguing over who did least, “You can't even say 'I'm sorry, Eva Smith.'” (the Inspector, Act 3), to which Sheila answers “That's the worst of it”.

check.prompt: Why does the warning about fire and blood and anguish land differently on an audience in 1945 than on the family in 1912?
check.solution: To the Birlings the words are a strange threat from a policeman. To the audience of 1945 they describe 1914 to 1918 and 1939 to 1945. Priestley set the play before the first war and staged it after the second so that the warning would be heard as something that had already come true.

steps.title: Who is he? The name, the knowledge, the exit
steps.body:
Priestley never says. The name sounds like *ghoul*; he knows things he could not know; he leaves before anyone thinks to doubt him; and the telephone at the end says a real inspector is on his way. Readers have called him a ghost, a conscience, a prophet, a figure of judgement, and Priestley's own voice, and the play supports each reading without settling on one.

**What the essay needs is not the answer but the effect.** Whatever he is, Priestley makes him unanswerable while he is on stage and unprovable once he has gone. That combination is the method: the family cannot argue with him, and afterwards they cannot be sure he was there, so what they do next is entirely their own choice.

**Use the readings, do not choose between them.** A sentence such as *whether he is read as a ghost or as Priestley's voice, the Inspector is built to be believed and then doubted* does more than a paragraph insisting he was a spirit.

check.prompt: The Inspector leaves the stage before anyone questions whether he is real. What is the effect of Priestley arranging it that way?
check.solution: Because no one doubts him while he speaks, the speech lands whole. The doubt that follows cannot undo it; it can only show which characters want an excuse. Priestley times the exit so that the message is safe and the family is tested.

steps.title: Eva Smith: the character who is never on stage
steps.body:
Eva Smith never appears. She is dead before the curtain rises, and everything the audience knows about her comes from the five people who harmed her and the one who is speaking for her. Priestley chose that, and it is one of the play's boldest methods.

**Three names, one life.** Eva Smith at the works and at Milwards; Daisy Renton in the Palace bar and with Gerald; Mrs Birling at the committee. Each name marks a door that was shut and a fresh start that failed. The Inspector's questioning puts the life back together in order.

**What she did.** She led a strike for higher wages; she refused money once she knew it was stolen. Priestley gives the girl the family treated as a nuisance the two most principled acts in the play.

**What she stands for.** The Inspector says it: “millions and millions and millions of Eva Smiths”. The commonest surname in the country and a first name that is nearly Eve. She is one girl and every girl, and the photograph that only one person sees at a time is how Priestley keeps her both.

visuals.alt: A flow chart of Eva Smith's life as the play reveals it: the works, the strike, Milwards, the Palace bar as Daisy Renton, the committee as Mrs Birling, and the Infirmary

check.solution: She helped lead the strike for higher wages, and she refused the money Eric gave her once she knew it was stolen. Priestley gives the absent girl the two cleanest acts in the play, so that the family who dismissed her as a nuisance are measured against her.

steps.title: Planning the June 2024 question on the Inspector
steps.body: The June 2024 paper asked how Priestley uses the Inspector to suggest the need for social change. The mark scheme's indicative content is a plan, and here it is turned into one.

visuals.problem: Turn the indicative content for the June 2024 Inspector question into an essay plan.

steps.text: AO1, what to cover: the family's and Gerald's attitudes to the girl; how each treated her; the Inspector's questioning of each; the revelations he brings to light.
steps.note: Whole text, in order: the chain, seen through the Inspector.

steps.text: AO2, the methods: his forensic questioning; the contrast between his directness and their evasiveness; the structural contrast before and after his arrival; the stage directions about him.
steps.note: Four methods named by the examiners. Use at least two.

steps.text: AO3, the ideas: boss and worker in a capitalist society; class and its effect on ordinary lives; how society could be organised differently; caring for one another.
steps.note: Four ideas, all carried by the speech.

steps.text: A paragraph, then: the Inspector's directness against Birling's evasion on the strike, with “Public men, Mr Birling, have responsibilities as well as privileges” as the evidence, ending on the idea of boss and worker.
steps.note: Method, quotation, idea, in one paragraph.

steps.text: The last paragraph: the speech, “We don't live alone. We are members of one body. We are responsible for each other”, set against Birling's speech in Act 1, and what a 1945 audience was being asked to choose.
steps.note: The thesis and the context, together.

steps.title: The Inspector and Priestley: whose voice?
steps.body:
The Inspector says what Priestley believed. Priestley co-founded the Common Wealth Party in 1942; his BBC radio Postscripts on Sunday nights in 1940 reached audiences of up to sixteen million and were taken off the air after complaints about their politics; and the play was written in the year the general election returned a Labour government to build a welfare state. The speech about one body is that politics, spoken on a stage.

**But he is not only a mouthpiece.** Priestley gives him a manner, a method, a timing and a name, and each of those is a choice about how the ideas reach the audience. A speech read aloud would be a lecture; the same words spoken by a man who has just taken a family apart, one link at a time, are a verdict.

**How to write it.** Context earns when it explains a choice. *Priestley, who had broadcast to millions in 1940 about the country that should follow the war, gives the Inspector a broadcaster's plainness* connects the life to the method. A paragraph about Priestley's career on its own does not.

rows: Speaks plainly, and speaks past the family to the audience
Helped found a party for a fairer settlement
Argues that society could be organised differently
Served in the first war and saw the second
Warns of fire and blood and anguish

check.prompt: Which sentence connects context to method in the way AO3 rewards?
check.solution: The sentence about the broadcaster's plainness takes one fact about the writer and uses it to explain one choice in the play. The list of dates is biography; the sentence calling the Inspector a socialist is a label; the sentence about the broadcasts being taken off the air is history with no play in it. Context that explains a method is the AO3 the scheme describes.

steps.title: The speech from memory
steps.body:
There is no extract for this text, so the speech has to be carried in. Try these before looking back.

1. Complete the line: *We don't live alone. We are members of one ...*
2. What are the three nouns in the warning about how the lesson will be taught?
3. What does the Inspector say each of them did, in the sentence that begins *each of you*?
4. What is the surname he gives to the millions?

Then write the whole of the one body line out, exactly, and check it against the lesson. It is the line every essay on this play can use.

steps.title: Writing about an absent character
steps.body:
Eva Smith is a device, and the strongest essays say so. Three moves make the paragraph.

**Name the absence as a choice.** Priestley keeps her off stage so that she can only be known through the people who harmed her; the audience judges them by how they describe her.

**Use the photograph.** Seen by one person at a time, it lets the Inspector prove each link and leaves the family a loophole. Priestley builds both the proof and the loophole into one object, and the loophole is a test the older characters fail.

**Read the names.** Eva, close to Eve; Smith, the commonest name there is; then Daisy Renton and Mrs Birling as the doors shut. The Inspector's millions turn one girl into everyone, and the argument of the play depends on that widening.

Write her as what Priestley does with her, and she becomes the strongest evidence in the essay rather than a name in a summary.

steps.title: The two who are not Birlings
steps.body:
The Inspector and the girl are the play's two outsiders, one on stage the whole time and one never on it, and Priestley builds the argument between them.

- **The Inspector's method:** one at a time, in order; the photograph shown singly; plain statements against evasions; arrives inside the speech, leaves before the doubt.
- **The speech:** each of you helped to kill her; millions of Eva Smiths; members of one body, responsible for each other; fire and blood and anguish.
- **What he is:** ghost, conscience, Priestley's voice, device; the essay needs the effect, not the answer.
- **Eva Smith:** never on stage; three names, three doors; the strike and the refused money; one girl and every girl.
- **The June 2024 question:** how Priestley uses the Inspector to suggest the need for social change; the scheme's methods are forensic questioning, directness against evasion, before and after, stage directions.

Learn the one body line exactly. It is the play's thesis, and it fits almost any question.

Seen singly, it protects the girl's privacy, and afterwards allows Gerald to identify her as Daisy Renton
Seen singly, it makes each character admit a link without comparing notes, and afterwards lets them claim it may have been different girls, which tests who wants an excuse

questions.prompt: Which two words in the Inspector's speech make the audience of 1945 hear the two world wars?
questions.solution: Fire and blood and anguish. Any pair of the three carries it: fire and blood are the wars, anguish is what followed them. Written in 1945 and set in 1912, the line is a prophecy to the family and a memory to the audience.

markScheme.description: fire and blood

questions.prompt: A paragraph on the Inspector as a device is built from these sentences. Put them in the order that runs from method to idea.
questions.solution: Method, then the contrast that carries the argument with its evidence, then the timing that protects the speech, then the idea for the audience. The idea comes last because the methods have earned it.

markScheme.description: the four sentences in order

items: Priestley gives the Inspector a method: the five questioned one at a time, in the order they met the girl, with the photograph seen singly
Set against the family's evasions, his plain statements carry the argument, as when he tells Birling that public men have responsibilities as well as privileges
Because the doubt about him is delayed until after his exit, the speech about one body is heard without suspicion
Through him Priestley puts to a 1945 audience the choice between Birling's self-interest and a society organised as one body

questions.prompt: How does Priestley use the Inspector to suggest the need for social change? Write one analytical paragraph that could sit in the middle of an answer to this June 2024 question, naming at least two of the methods the mark scheme lists and connecting them to the ideas it lists.
questions.skill: planning an essay on the Inspector
questions.solution: Priestley makes the Inspector's method carry his argument. The questioning is forensic: the five are taken one at a time, in the order they met the girl, and no link is left until it is admitted, so the audience watches a life being reassembled from the doors that were shut in it. Against that method Priestley sets the family's evasions, and the contrast is where the ideas live. When Birling reminds the Inspector that he is a public man, the reply is not an argument but a statement, “Public men, Mr Birling, have responsibilities as well as privileges”, and the plainness of the sentence, beside Birling's bluster about the strike, makes the case about boss and worker without a speech. The structural contrast before and after his arrival does the same work on a larger scale: the room that held a celebration of prosperity holds an inquiry into what that prosperity cost, and nothing has changed but the presence of one man asking questions. By the time the Inspector says that “We don't live alone. We are members of one body. We are responsible for each other”, the audience has seen the alternative in action for two acts, and the line lands as a conclusion rather than a slogan. For an audience in 1945, choosing what kind of country to rebuild, Priestley uses the Inspector to make the need for change something that has been demonstrated, one link at a time, before it is stated.

questions.prompt: How does Priestley present Eva Smith, a character who never appears on stage? Write one analytical paragraph on her as a device: her absence, her names, the photograph, and what she is used to show about the family and about 1912.
questions.solution: Priestley keeps Eva Smith off the stage, and the absence is his first method: she can be known only through the five people who harmed her, so every description of her is evidence against the describer. Mrs Birling's contempt and Gerald's fondness tell the audience about Mrs Birling and Gerald. Her names do the work of a plot: Eva Smith at the works and the shop, Daisy Renton in the bar, Mrs Birling at the committee, each a door shut and a fresh start that failed, and the Inspector's questioning puts the life back together in the order it was taken apart. The photograph, shown to one person at a time, is her presence on stage, and Priestley builds it to prove each link while the Inspector is there and to offer a loophole once he has gone, so that the family's last act is to choose whether she was one girl or several. Against all of this Priestley gives her the two cleanest acts in the play, the strike for higher wages and the refusal of stolen money, so that the people who dismissed her are measured by her. When the Inspector speaks of “millions and millions and millions of Eva Smiths and John Smiths”, the commonest name in the country turns one girl into every working person, and the play's argument about class and responsibility is made through a character the audience never sees, which is why it cannot be argued with.

questions.prompt: Sheila says of the Inspector that he knows, before he has questioned her mother. What is Priestley doing with that line?
questions.solution: The line places Sheila on the Inspector's side of the method: she has seen that evasion is useless and that the wall her mother is building will be broken. The audience is warned, and the dramatic irony of the trap depends on the warning.

markScheme.description: Making Sheila the character who understands the Inspector's method, so that the audience is shown the trap before Mrs Birling walks into it

options: Making Sheila the character who understands the Inspector's method, so that the audience is shown the trap before Mrs Birling walks into it
Showing that Sheila is frightened of the police and wants her mother to confess quickly

questions.prompt: A student claims: 'The ending proves the Inspector was a ghost.' Which is the better account of what the ending does?
questions.solution: The play refuses to settle it, and the refusal is the method. If the Inspector were proved real, the family would have no choice; if proved false, the audience could dismiss him. Left open, the doubt sorts the characters by what they want to believe.

markScheme.description: It leaves his nature open, so that what each character does with the doubt, rather than the answer, is what the last scene reveals

options: It proves he was a ghost, since a real inspector is on his way and two inspectors cannot investigate one death
It leaves his nature open, so that what each character does with the doubt, rather than the answer, is what the last scene reveals
It proves he was a fraud, since the police sergeant has never heard of him, the Infirmary has no body and the family were taken in by a stranger
It proves he was Priestley himself, since only the writer could know what the family had done

examTechnique.body:
**The Inspector is a device.** A question on him asks how Priestley uses him, and the June 2024 mark scheme names the methods: forensic questioning, directness against the family's evasiveness, the structural contrast before and after his arrival, the stage directions. Take two, name them, and say what each does.

**Learn the speech in pieces.** Verdict, scale, principle, warning. The one body line must be exact.

**Do not decide what he is.** Ghost, conscience, Priestley's voice, device: the play keeps it open, and the mark is for the effect of the uncertainty on the family and the audience.

**Eva Smith is a method.** Her absence, her names, the photograph and her two principled acts are choices Priestley made. Write about what they do, not about how sad her story is.

**Context that explains.** Priestley's broadcasts, his party and the 1945 election earn when they explain a choice in the play, not as a paragraph on their own.
examinerErrors: Describing the Inspector as mysterious or powerful without naming a method by which Priestley makes him so.
Spending the essay arguing that he is a ghost, when the question asked what Priestley uses him for.
Misquoting the speech, especially the one body line, which is the most-quoted line in the play and the easiest to get wrong.
Writing about Eva Smith with sympathy but without method: what she suffered, rather than what Priestley does with her absence.
Treating the photograph as a plot detail rather than as the object that both proves the chain and offers the loophole.
Giving Priestley's biography as context without connecting a single fact of it to a choice in the play.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer treats the Inspector as Priestley's instrument and says exactly how the instrument works: the order of the questioning as a proof, the plain statements as a contrast with the family's evasions, the exit timed so that the speech is heard straight and the doubt tests the family. It quotes the speech exactly and knows what each piece of it does. It reads Eva Smith as an absence built on purpose, with the photograph and the names as methods, and it connects both characters to the choice Priestley put before an audience in 1945 without a paragraph of biography. It does not decide what the Inspector is; it shows what the uncertainty is for.
